new_statements.translation: (p. 91, §4 Tone) The suprasegmental phonemes of Northern Barasano comprise high tone (marked /´/ over the vowel) and low tone (unmarked). [...] In disyllabic words all the contrastable tone patterns have been observed: [HH, HL, LH, LL]. In trisyllables all possible tone patterns have been observed except [LLH]. There appears to be no restriction on tone patterns in words of more than three syllables. (p. 92) High tone and stress always coincide. There may be multiple stress within the word. In long utterances, as in narratives, the stress-tone features are frequently lost.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a record for 'Barasano del norte' with an EMPTY rule and no existing statements, so this source fills it rather than agreeing or contradicting: the language is tonal (two level tones) and stress is bound to high tone, multiple per word, with no fixed position. Consistent with WALS 13A (Waimaha = simple tone system, coded from Stolte & Stolte 1971). Note the 1976 text is the Spanish version of the 1971 Linguistics article; pp. 84-86 (§§1-2, syllable and word structure) were not in the open excerpts.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Northern Barasano is a two-tone language (H marked with acute, L unmarked). Stress is not an independent word-level category: it always falls on high-toned syllables ('el tono alto y el acento coinciden siempre'), and since a word may carry several high tones it may carry several stresses ('acento múltiple'). Tone/stress placement is lexically free: all four patterns occur in disyllables, all trisyllabic patterns except LLH occur, and no restriction is reported for longer words, so there is no fixed stress position. Final tone patterns are grammatically predictable (fn. 7: low rises above preceding highs in dependent clauses). Phonetic detail: utterance-initial low rises slightly; utterance-final high is somewhat lower than preceding highs; a low between two highs is nearer mid.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary distinction is made; the authors state only that multiple stresses can occur in one word (one per high-toned syllable), producing a 'monotonía' effect when three highs or three lows follow each other.
new_statements.exceptions: In long utterances such as narratives the stress-tone features are frequently lost and the speaker levels to monotone except for final grammatical intonation (declarative falling, interrogative rising, dependent-clause short rising, fn. 8). Lengthened vowels are analysed as V.V sequences partly because they often carry two tone levels (§3.9). The orthography (p. 93) writes the acute for 'tono alto y acento' only where needed to avoid ambiguity.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes 'barasano del norte' = the waimajã / Waimaha (bará) of the Colombian Vaupés (clans cawayaria, wamatanara, wanaco bara, pamoa bara on the Tiquié, Colorado, Yapú and Inambú), main consultant Feliciano, c. 500 speakers (p. 83, §0). The authors state explicitly that Northern Barasano and Southern Barasano (the Panerã, Eduria, Comia clans, i.e. Barasana proper) 'hablan dos idiomas distintos que no son dialectos del mismo idioma', so the statements belong to waim1255 and not to Barasana (bara1380).

new_statements.relation_note: Same work as the catalog's source (the catalog record 'tonal' for Barasano del norte quotes this Spanish version, pp. 87 and 91-92); the complete copy confirms the quoted sentences verbatim on the page renders and adds only §1 p. 85 (every syllable high or low tone; demarcative crescendo on syllables 1-2), which was missing from the Rosetta excerpts and does not change the classification. The 1971 English original was not opened (paywalled); fn. 2 identifies the Spanish text as its republication.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Northern Barasano (Waimaja) is analysed as a two-tone language: every syllable of the phonological word (1-7 syllables, p. 85) bears phonemic high or low tone, all four patterns contrast on disyllables and 7 of 8 on trisyllables, with no restriction on longer words. 'Accent' is not an independent, positionally fixed word stress: it always coincides with high tone, a word may carry several accents, and the orthographic acute marks 'tono alto y acento' together (p. 93). No syllable position is singled out for stress. §1 (p. 85) adds a demarcative cue: in words of two or more syllables a rapid crescendo over the first and second syllables with decrescendo afterwards, and final-vowel devoicing at the word boundary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; 'Puede haber acento múltiple en la palabra' (p. 92) = several equal accents, one per high-toned syllable, not a primary/secondary hierarchy.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 7 (p. 91): word-final tone patterns are grammatically predictable; in dependent clauses a low tone rises above preceding highs and lengthened vowels with falling tone occur on verb roots (grammatically conditioned). p. 92 'En expresiones largas, como en las narraciones, los rasgos de acento-tono se pierden con frecuencia' + fn. 8: speech levels to monotone except for the final grammatical intonation contours (declarative falling, interrogative rising, dependent clause short rise). p. 91 §3.9: long vowels = VV sequences, often with two tone levels. p. 93: the acute is written only where needed to avoid ambiguity.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Northern Barasano = Waimaja ('waimaja', self-designation; formerly 'bará'), Eastern Tucanoan, data from Caño Colorado (clan wamutañara area), March-November 1966, with some consultants from the eastern (Tiquié) dialect; fn. 1 states that Northern and Southern Barasano (panerá, eduria, comia clans = bara1380) are distinct languages, so the copy's storage under the bara1380 folder is a filing accident of the earlier bundle, not a statement about Barasana-Eduria.

tone_statements.quote: The languages we will focus on belong to the Tukanoan family, represented in the types proposed by Hyman as follows: /H, L/ Barasana, Tatuyo, Wanano /H, Ø/ (i) Tuyuka (ii) Koreguaje?, Kubeo?, Tanimuka ? L, Ø/ None /H, L, Ø/ Maihiki (Orejon) /?/ Waimaha, Tukano. First, I will show how the languages in the /H, L/ type differ both by the grammatical use of tone and by the kind of processes they appeal to [2, 3, 9]. Then I will reinterpret the Kubeo [1] and Tukano [8] data in order to remove the /?/ from their present classification. Finally, I will try to include the remaining Tukanoan languages into Hyman’s groups, using available descriptions not surveyed by Hyman [4].

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim against the PDF we hold's text (pp. 87, 91) and a rendered page scan (p. 92); the deciding sentence 'El tono alto y el acento coinciden siempre. Puede haber acento múltiple en la palabra.' is exactly as cited. (2) The classification rests on a 1976 SIL phonemic sketch (Spanish version of the 1971 Linguistics article) — short and impressionistic, but it is the only phonological description of Waimaha that exists: Glottolog lists no grammar and no other phonology, and WALS 13A and SAPhon both derive from the same Stolte work; Crossref, BDTD and HAL show nothing newer. (3) downloaded now from archive.org the two remaining Rosetta excerpts (p. 83 intro; p. 93 orthography): p. 93 glosses the acute as 'tono alto y acento', confirming that prominence is lexical high tone, i.e. tonal-OR-pitch accent with no positional stress rule. pp. 84-86 remain unheld; no open cop
